_about: Question bank clean-up. Each question is named by one of its wrong options' ids, which is how it was exported. Applied with scripts.apply_question_fixes.

retire.reason: faulty: Answer key is wrong: with C fixed, A = Cd/ε₀, so reducing d needs a SMALLER area. The option marked wrong ('decreases') is correct
faulty: Option 86, marked wrong, is a correct reason: d² << A keeps fringing negligible so the field is uniform
faulty: Two answers say the same thing: correct 'increase by a factor of 2' and wrong 'It would double'
faulty: False premise: two parallel wires with currents in the same direction attract; the force between them is not zero
faulty: Says a proton and an electron in the same downward field both feel a downward force; the electron is pushed upward, so the 'wrong' option about opposite forces is true

faulty: Key is wrong and contradicts the first radial-field question: a radial field keeps the field IN the coil's plane (perpendicular to the wires), not perpendicular to the plane. Option 170, marked wrong, is correct: a uniform field would make the torque depend on angle
faulty: Option 231, marked wrong, is correct (r parallel to dl makes the cross product zero); its own note admits the student 'correctly identifies' this
faulty: Option 236, marked wrong, is the right formula: with θ = 0 it gives zero, the same as the key
faulty: Option 237, marked wrong, is correct; its own note says 'both are correct'
faulty: Option 248, marked wrong, is correct (ω = qB/m has no speed in it) -- its own note calls it 'correct reasoning'
faulty: Option 265, marked wrong, is a valid argument: a field component along the surface would change the potential along it, contradicting the definition
faulty: Option 271, marked wrong, is essentially correct: the potential changes only along the normal
faulty: Key gets the reason backwards: inside, the field is along the axis, so it is perpendicular to the transverse sections; B·dl is zero there because the field has no component ALONG them
faulty: Option 290, marked wrong, states the correct mechanism: charge leaving one plate enters the next, by conservation of charge
faulty: Key says the cube network is solved with series and parallel rules; it is not reducible that way -- NCERT uses symmetry and Kirchhoff's rules, so option 311 is closer to right
faulty: False premise: asks why the current splits UNEQUALLY at the cube's entry corner. By symmetry it splits equally, I/3 in each resistor
faulty: Says doubling the distance quarters the potential 'because it is inversely proportional to distance'. V ∝ 1/r, so it halves: the option marked wrong (one-half) is the right answer
faulty: Option 352, marked wrong, is essentially the right reason: the air gap's unchanged field keeps the voltage drop smaller than with a full slab
faulty: Option 389, marked wrong, is a correct explanation: zero enclosed charge inside, all of q enclosed outside -- the same as the 'correct' answer in other words
